section_titles: Parts and Wholes — Halves
periods.activity_title: Folding Fair: Who Got Equal Shares?

tasks_in_class.description: Discuss which part of the paper you would have chosen (half or two quarters) and why; try with paper; reason about equal division and Samina's choice.
Colour the figures that Samina has divided into halves correctly; explain how you got the answer.
Divide the given shapes into halves by drawing a line.

time_bands.activity: Each pair receives a sheet of paper. Students fold it in two different ways — once lengthwise, once diagonally — and hold up the results. The class discusses: are both folds fair? Do both halves match when you flip one on top of the other?

Let Us Discuss Q1–4, p.62 ("Discuss which part of the paper you would have chosen....") — Teacher reads the Ikra-and-Samina scenario aloud. Pairs try the fold with real paper, then share which choice they would make and why. Class settles on what 'equal' means.

Let Us Do Q1, p.63 ("Colour the figures that Samina has divided into halves....") — Students work individually, colouring and writing a one-phrase reason. Two or three pupils explain their thinking to the class.

Let Us Do Q2, p.63 ("Divide the given shapes into halves by drawing a line.") — Students draw lines on the printed shapes. Pairs compare their lines: do they agree? Is there more than one correct line for any shape? A quick show of hands closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who fold a shape asymmetrically and still call it 'halves' — the core misconception here is that two pieces must look the same, not merely be equal in amount. Encourage students to physically overlap the parts to verify equality, rather than judging by eye. A common error is drawing a line that splits the figure into two visually distinct pieces that are not equal in area.
materials: A4 or scrap paper (one sheet per pair)

section_titles: Many Ways to Make Halves and Quarters
periods.activity_title: One Rectangle, Many Cuts — Halves and Quarters

tasks_in_class.description: Fold/cut a rectangular paper into two equal parts in as many different ways as you can; try with actual paper.
Draw and show five different ways to fold/cut a rectangle into four equal parts (1/4 or quarter).
Divide the given shapes (diamond, rectangle, oval, L-shape, cross-shape) into 4 equal parts/quarters.

homework.description: Match the given part-shapes (hourglass, triangle, semicircle, rectangle) with their corresponding whole shapes using the 1/2 and 1/4 labels.

time_bands.activity: Each student gets two rectangular paper strips. Students fold the first into halves in as many ways as they can discover, recording each fold type by tracing the fold line on a small sketch. The class pools all the different fold lines found — vertical, horizontal, diagonal — and discusses: are all of them truly equal halves?

Let Us Try Q1, p.64 ("Fold/cut a rectangular paper into two equal parts....") and Let Us Try Q2, p.65 ("Draw and show five different ways to fold/cut a rectangle into four equal parts....") — Students use the second paper strip to find quarter-folds. They sketch each way in their notebooks, labelling each part 1/4. Groups compare and see whether they found the same five ways.

Let Us Try Q3, p.64 ("Divide the given shapes (diamond, rectangle, oval, L-shape, cross-shape) into 4 equal parts/quarters.") — Students work on the printed shapes, drawing dividing lines. The teacher circulates and asks: 'How do you know these four parts are equal?' Students who finish early attempt to find a second way to quarter the same shape.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have worked with the idea that one half means two equal parts of a whole are now extending that understanding to quarters and to the idea that equal parts can look different from one another depending on how the cut is made. Watch for the error of dividing an irregular shape (L-shape, cross) into four pieces that are visually symmetrical but not truly equal in area — encourage folding or counting squares to check. The homework matching task reinforces that a part-shape implies a specific whole.

section_titles: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
periods.activity_title: Dhokla for All: More Guests, Smaller Shares

tasks_in_class.description: Observe Sumedha's share as each guest arrives; reason about 9 vs 11 people; how many 1/6 pieces make a whole; Sumedha's share if two guests give theirs back.
How much dhokla per person when shared equally among 6 and among 8 people? Who gets bigger pieces? Draw and explain.
Shade the dhokla circles to show Sumedha's share for 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, and 9 people; discuss why fractions get smaller as people increase.

time_bands.activity: Teacher tells the dhokla story orally: Sumedha is about to eat, then guests keep arriving one by one. Students listen and predict: when a second person arrives, what happens to each person's share? Hands go up; students reason aloud.

Let Us Discuss Q1–4, p.68 ("Observe Sumedha's share as each guest arrives; reason about 9 vs 11 people....") — Teacher leads a whole-class discussion, asking students to name the fraction at each stage (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, …). Students write the fractions in their notebooks. The question about two guests returning prompts quiet think-time, then pair-share.

Let Us Do Q1, p.68 ("How much dhokla per person when shared equally among 6 and among 8 people?....") — Students draw two circles in their notebooks, divide them into 6 and 8 equal parts respectively, and shade one part each. They write a sentence comparing the two shares.

Let Us Do Q2, p.69 ("Shade the dhokla circles to show Sumedha's share for 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, and 9 people....") — Students shade the printed circles. Teacher asks: 'As the number of people grows, what happens to the shaded slice?' Students articulate the inverse pattern in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The central insight — that a larger denominator means a smaller share — is counterintuitive for many students who expect bigger numbers to mean bigger quantities. Having students physically shade and compare circles where 1/8 is visibly smaller than 1/3 makes this concrete before any symbolic rule is stated. A common error is writing 1/9 > 1/6 because 9 > 6; encourage students to look at their shaded circles rather than comparing digits.

section_titles: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
periods.activity_title: Fraction Kit: Seeing and Comparing Unit Fractions

tasks_in_class.description: Use fraction kit to share observations about pieces and wholes; compare two pieces; verify that 5 pieces of 1/5 make a whole; explain why a given piece is one-third.
Fill in blanks to compare unit fractions: which is greater among 1/5 and 1/4; compare 1/9 and 1/6; compare 1/6 and 1/8; choose a pair where one is smaller.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes or directs students to the fraction kit in the textbook. Students cut out (or simply handle) the fraction strips and lay the 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 pieces side by side on their desks. A brief silent observation: what do they notice about the sizes?

Let Us Discuss Q1–5, p.69 ("Use fraction kit to share observations about pieces and wholes; compare two pieces; verify that 5 pieces of 1/5 make a whole; explain why a given piece is one-third.") — Students work in pairs, physically placing pieces next to each other. Teacher circulates and asks: 'How many 1/5 pieces line up to match the whole strip? How do you know that piece is one-third?' Pairs share findings with the class.

Let Us Discuss fill-in-blanks, p.70 ("Fill in blanks to compare unit fractions: which is greater among 1/5 and 1/4; compare 1/9 and 1/6; compare 1/6 and 1/8....") — Students write their comparisons, using the fraction kit pieces as evidence where possible. Teacher invites one student per comparison to share the reasoning: 'I know 1/4 > 1/5 because when I placed both pieces, the 1/4 piece is longer.' Class discusses the pattern that emerges.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the dhokla shading in which students observed that more people means smaller pieces, this unit gives students a physical fraction kit to verify comparisons through direct measurement. The key error to watch: students who compare fractions by reading the numerator or denominator as a standalone number rather than as a part-of-whole relationship. Ask 'which piece is bigger when you hold them?' to anchor the comparison in the concrete model.
materials: Fraction kit from textbook (cut-out strips) or teacher-prepared fraction strips
Scissors if kits are not pre-cut

section_titles: My Flower Garden — Non-unit Fractions
periods.activity_title: Garden Plots: Naming Parts Greater Than One

tasks_in_class.description: Make a flower garden with 7 plots: (a) Marigold in 1/7, Rose and Hibiscus in 3/7 each; (b) Lily in 3/7, Marigold in 2/7, Periwinkle in 2/7; (c) Mogra in 5/7, Hibiscus in 2/7.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a strip of five boxes on the board — Idha's flower garden row from the chapter text. The class reads the garden story together (p.71). Teacher fills the first box with 'Rose', asks: 'What fraction of the garden is roses?' Students answer 1/5. Teacher fills three boxes: 'Now?' Students say 3/5. The class establishes: numerator counts the coloured plots, denominator counts all plots. Teacher introduces the term 'non-unit fraction' in plain words: a fraction where more than one part is counted.

Let Us Do Q(a)(b)(c), p.71 ("Make a flower garden with 7 plots: (a) Marigold in 1/7, Rose and Hibiscus in 3/7 each; (b) Lily in 3/7, Marigold in 2/7, Periwinkle in 2/7; (c) Mogra in 5/7, Hibiscus in 2/7.") — Students draw a seven-box strip for each of the three gardens, colour the boxes with the specified flowers, and write the fraction labels beneath each. Teacher circulates; for part (c) students check: 5/7 + 2/7 — do all seven boxes get filled? What does 7/7 mean? A brief whole-class check closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who are comfortable with unit fractions (one part of a whole) can trip over non-unit fractions because they do not immediately see that the numerator simply counts the number of equal parts being referred to. Having students colour and label each box individually before writing the fraction ensures the counting is explicit. Watch for the error of writing 3/5 when there are 7 total boxes — students sometimes carry over the earlier five-plot garden and forget to use the actual denominator of the new garden.
materials: Crayons (at least three colours per student)
Rulers (to draw clean strip boxes if needed)

section_titles: Dream Dosa Designer — Fractions of a Whole and Collection
periods.activity_title: Dosa Fractions: Circles, Sectors, and Diyas

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Do It Yourself Q1–4 (four dosas), p.73
tasks_in_class.description: Write the fractions for each topping in four given dosas (sectors marked with numbers show part size).
Make a dosa with 2/3 spicy onion and 1/3 classic potato; make another with 3/8 classic potato, 1/8 chilly paneer, 4/8 tangy tomato.
Meena has 8 diyas — divide into 4 equal groups to find 1/4; colour 2 diyas red.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a large circle on the board, divides it into 4 equal sectors, labels one sector with a topping name. Students state the fraction for that topping (1/4). Teacher adds another sector of the same topping: students call out 2/4. The class discusses: the whole dosa is one circle — what fraction is un-topped? This brief opener connects the circular model to fraction notation.

Do It Yourself Q1–4 (four dosas), p.73 ("Write the fractions for each topping in four given dosas....") — Students look at the four printed dosa circles and write the fraction for each topping sector beside it. Teacher checks that students count the number of sectors correctly and uses the total number of sectors as the denominator.

Let Us Explore, p.73 ("Make a dosa with 2/3 spicy onion and 1/3 classic potato; make another with 3/8 classic potato, 1/8 chilly paneer, 4/8 tangy tomato.") — Students draw two blank circles, divide and colour according to the specifications, then label each sector. Pairs compare their dosas and check: do all the fractions add up to cover the whole circle?

Let Us Explore (diyas), p.73 ("Meena has 8 diyas — divide into 4 equal groups to find 1/4; colour 2 diyas red.") — Students draw 8 small diya symbols, circle groups of 2 to show four equal groups, and identify that one group is 1/4. Teacher asks: 'How many diyas is 1/4 of 8?' Students write: 1/4 of 8 = 2. The class discusses how a fraction of a collection differs from a fraction of a shape.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit bridges two models of fractions: the continuous circular model (dosa sectors) and the discrete collection model (8 diyas). Students sometimes struggle with the discrete model because they expect fractions to live on shapes rather than on groups of objects — the diya grouping directly addresses this. A common error is treating 1/4 of 8 as 4 (reading the denominator as the answer) rather than dividing 8 into 4 equal groups and counting one group.

section_titles: Fractions in Our Surroundings — Collections
periods.activity_title: Sharing Cookies and Counting Pots: Fractions Around Us

tasks_in_class.description: 12 cookies shared equally; find the fraction each child gets for 3, 6, 2, and 4 children.
Place hairbands on 1/3 of Simran's 9 school friends shown in a picture.
Draw flowers in 1/5 of each given group of pots (groups of 5, 10, 15 pots).

time_bands.activity: Teacher places 12 counters (or draws 12 circles on the board) and asks two students to come up and share them equally. The class identifies: each person gets 6, which is 1/2 of 12. Teacher repeats with 3 students: each gets 4, which is 1/3 of 12. The class articulates the connection between equal sharing and fraction notation.

Let Us Do Q1(a–d), p.74 ("12 cookies shared equally; find the fraction each child gets for 3, 6, 2, and 4 children.") — Students draw 12 cookie symbols, draw loops to show equal groups for each sharing scenario, and write the fraction. Teacher asks after each: 'What is the denominator? What does it tell us?'

Let Us Do Q5, p.74 ("Place hairbands on 1/3 of Simran's 9 school friends shown in a picture.") — Students count 9 friends, circle groups of 3, and mark hairbands on one group. They write: 1/3 of 9 = 3.

Let Us Do Q6, p.74 ("Draw flowers in 1/5 of each given group of pots (groups of 5, 10, 15 pots).") — Students identify 1/5 of 5, 1/5 of 10, 1/5 of 15 by circling groups and drawing flowers. Teacher asks: 'Why does 1/5 of 15 give more flowers than 1/5 of 5?' Students explain in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who understand fractions of shapes sometimes struggle to apply the same logic to discrete collections because there is no shape to fold. Having students draw loops around equal groups makes the division visible and concrete. The typical error is writing the total count as the answer rather than the count in one group — for example, writing '9' rather than '3' for 1/3 of 9.
materials: Counters or small tokens (12 per pair, for the opener)

section_titles: Fractions in Our Surroundings — Collections
periods.activity_title: Barfis, Ribbons, and Real-World Fraction Reasoning

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Find Fractions Q1, p.75
tasks_in_class.description: 16 barfis divided into 4 equal parts — draw the picture and find how many barfis are in 1/4.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Find Fractions Q2, p.75
tasks_in_class.description: Mohan's ribbon is 1/4 as long as Rohan's; given Mohan's ribbon length, draw how long Rohan's ribbon would be.
Observe your surroundings and write two situations where fractions are used.

time_bands.activity: Teacher places 16 counters in a row on the board and asks: 'If I want to divide these into 4 equal groups, how many go in each group?' Students count aloud and arrive at 4 per group. Teacher asks: 'So 1/4 of 16 is…?' Students answer and the teacher writes 1/4 × 16 = 4 in plain words.

Let Us Find Fractions Q1, p.75 ("16 barfis divided into 4 equal parts — draw the picture and find how many barfis are in 1/4.") — Students draw 16 barfi shapes in a row, loop off groups of 4, and write the answer. Teacher circulates and checks that groups are equal.

Let Us Find Fractions Q2, p.75 ("Mohan's ribbon is 1/4 as long as Rohan's; given Mohan's ribbon length, draw how long Rohan's ribbon would be.") — Students draw Mohan's ribbon as a short strip, then draw Rohan's ribbon by repeating that length four times. Teacher asks: 'If Mohan's ribbon is 3 cm, how long is Rohan's? How do you know?'

Try Yourself, p.75 ("Observe your surroundings and write two situations where fractions are used.") — Students look around the room or think of home situations and write two examples in complete sentences. A few students share; the class evaluates whether each example is genuinely a fraction of a whole or a collection.

periods.teacher_notes: The ribbon task flips the usual direction: students are given the part and must find the whole, which is the inverse of fraction-of-a-collection. Many students attempt to divide the given length rather than multiply it — encourage them to re-read 'Mohan's ribbon is 1/4 of Rohan's' and ask who has the longer ribbon. The 'Try Yourself' observation task links fractions to lived experience and surfaces informal fraction language students already use.

section_titles: Equivalent Fractions through Paper Folding
periods.activity_title: Folding Into Thirds, Then Smaller and Smaller

tasks_in_class.description: Fold paper into thirds, colour one third, fold in half repeatedly; observe and write the fraction after each fold: 1/3 = 2/6 = ___ = ___ = ___.
Fold a new paper starting with two equal parts, halving each time; fill in: 1/2 = 2/4 = ___ = ___ = ___.

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up a rectangular strip and folds it into three equal parts, opens it, and asks: 'How many parts? What fraction is one part?' Students answer 1/3. Teacher shades one part with a marker. 'The shaded amount is 1/3 of the strip.' This establishes the starting point.

Let Us Do Q1–6, p.76 ("Fold paper into thirds, colour one third, fold in half repeatedly; observe and write the fraction after each fold: 1/3 = 2/6 = ___ = ___ = ___.") — Each student folds their own strip. After folding in half once, they open it and count: how many equal parts now? How many are coloured? They write 2/6. They fold again (into quarters of the original third), open, count, and write 4/12. The chain grows on the page.

Let Us Try, p.77 ("Fold a new paper starting with two equal parts, halving each time; fill in: 1/2 = 2/4 = ___ = ___ = ___.") — Students repeat the process with a fresh strip starting from halves. They build the equivalence chain. The teacher brings the two chains to the board side by side and asks: 'What pattern do you notice each time we fold in half?' Students articulate: both numerator and denominator double.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the first time students encounter equivalent fractions, though the term is introduced gently through the physical action of folding. The key observation — that colouring stays the same while the denominator grows — is best drawn out by asking students to hold the strip up to a window: the coloured portion has not changed, only the number of lines on it. Watch for students who miscount the total parts after multiple folds; having them trace each crease line clearly before counting helps.
materials: Paper strips (two per student, long rectangular pieces)

section_titles: Equivalent Fractions through Paper Folding
periods.activity_title: Fraction Chart: Comparing and Checking Equivalences

tasks_in_class.description: Using the fraction chart: how many 1/4 equal 1/2; is 2/3 greater than 1/2; do ten 1/10 make a whole; do three 1/6 equal two 1/8; how many 1/8 make 1/4; find pieces that combine into a bigger piece.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays or sketches the fraction chart (rows showing 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, … 1/10) on the board. Students open their textbooks to p.77. The class reads the chart together: each row is a whole divided into equal pieces of different sizes. Teacher points to the 1/4 row: 'How many 1/4 pieces fill the whole? How can we check using the chart?'

Let Us Discuss Q1–6, p.77 ("Using the fraction chart: how many 1/4 equal 1/2; is 2/3 greater than 1/2; do ten 1/10 make a whole; do three 1/6 equal two 1/8; how many 1/8 make 1/4; find pieces that combine into a bigger piece.") — Students work through each question, using the chart as the evidence base. After each question the teacher invites a student to explain their reasoning: 'How do you know? Where on the chart did you look?' The class gives particular attention to the question 'do three 1/6 equal two 1/8?' — students place imaginary pieces on the chart and discover they do not align.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who did the paper-folding in the previous unit are now using the printed fraction chart as a visual record of the same relationships. The key challenge in this unit is the comparison question 'do three 1/6 equal two 1/8?' — many students guess yes because both expressions have the same structure. Encourage students to line up the chart rows physically and compare lengths. The last question (find pieces that combine into a bigger piece) opens a rich conversation about equivalent fractions and is worth spending extra time on if the class is ready.
materials: Fraction strips or cut-outs from the fraction kit (optional)

section_titles: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
periods.activity_title: Equal Parts or Not? Checking Fraction Claims in Shapes

tasks_in_class.description: Bablu's squares — circle the ones cut into equal parts; write the fraction for the shaded part wherever possible.
Check whether Ameena, Kishore, Perry, Kunj, Balu, and Gita's fraction claims for shaded regions are correct; circle correct ones, cross out incorrect; draw lines to make parts equal if needed.
Identify the fractions represented by the coloured parts in three given grid pictures (triangles in squares).

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws two squares on the board: one cut into two equal rectangles, another cut into two unequal pieces. 'Both are cut in two. Can I call each a half?' Students discuss. The class establishes: equal parts are necessary for a fraction to be named. This frames the work ahead.

Let Us Do Q1, p.78 ("Bablu's squares — circle the ones cut into equal parts; write the fraction for the shaded part wherever possible.") — Students examine Bablu's set of squares, decide which are genuinely equal-parted, circle them, and write the fraction for the shaded region. Those not worth circling get a cross. The class compares answers and talks through any disagreements.

Let Us Do Q2, p.78 ("Check whether Ameena, Kishore, Perry, Kunj, Balu, and Gita's fraction claims for shaded regions are correct; circle correct ones, cross out incorrect; draw lines to make parts equal if needed.") — Students work through each person's shape, verifying the claim. Where the parts are not yet equal, they redraw dividing lines to show how it could be corrected.

Let Us Do Q3, p.79 ("Identify the fractions represented by the coloured parts in three given grid pictures (triangles in squares).") — Students count total triangular cells and shaded cells to write the fraction. Teacher asks: 'Does the shape of the shaded part change the fraction, or does only the count matter?'

periods.teacher_notes: The central skill in this unit is verifying whether a claimed fraction is valid — not just reading a given fraction but evaluating one. Watch for students who accept any division of a shape into the right number of pieces as valid, without checking that the pieces are equal in area. Encouraging students to trace or overlay the parts is more effective than asking them to judge by eye, particularly for irregular shapes like triangles cut from squares.
materials: Pencils and rulers (for redrawing lines in Q2)

section_titles: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
periods.activity_title: Pattern Blocks and Shading: Reading and Making Fractions

tasks_in_class.description: Identify the fraction of the whole that the blue parts make in each of three pattern-block pictures (hexagons, diamonds, arrow shapes).
Divide the given shapes and shade the appropriate parts: shade 2/3 of rectangle, 4/6 of circle, 1/4 of cross-shape (also show 1/8), 3/4 of L-shape.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple arrangement of four hexagons on the board, two of them shaded. 'I have four hexagons; two are blue. What fraction is blue?' Students answer 2/4. Teacher rearranges the same shapes into a different pattern and repeats. The class observes: the fraction depends on counting, not on arrangement.

Let Us Do Q4, p.79 ("Identify the fraction of the whole that the blue parts make in each of three pattern-block pictures (hexagons, diamonds, arrow shapes).") — Students count total pieces and blue pieces for each picture, writing the fraction. Teacher asks for each: 'What is the whole? What are you counting as the parts?'

Let Us Do Q5, p.79 ("Divide the given shapes and shade the appropriate parts: shade 2/3 of rectangle, 4/6 of circle, 1/4 of cross-shape (also show 1/8), 3/4 of L-shape.") — Students divide each shape by drawing lines, then shade the required fraction. Teacher circulates; for the cross-shape (1/4 and then 1/8) students must first make 4 equal parts, then subdivide to show eighths. A closing pair-share: students check each other's shaded shapes.

periods.teacher_notes: The pattern-block task requires students to identify the 'whole collection' as the total number of blocks, not just one shape — this is the same discrete-collection thinking practiced in the fractions-in-surroundings section, now applied to geometric arrangements. The shading task (Q5) is a productive inverse of reading: students must decide how to divide the shape before shading. Watch for students who shade 4/6 of the circle differently from 2/3 — this surfaces equivalent-fraction intuition from the paper-folding work.
materials: Rulers and compass or circular stencil (for dividing circle)

periods.activity_title: Fractions All Around: A Whole-Chapter Gallery and Relay

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a single large circle on the board and asks the class to call out every fraction concept they associate with it: half, quarter, thirds, unit fractions, non-unit fractions, shading, equivalence. The teacher writes each concept as a label around the circle, creating a visual map of the chapter's ideas. No new concepts are introduced; this is a retrieval opener.

Fraction Relay (four rounds, two minutes each): the teacher poses one question per round drawn from across the chapter — (1) 'Write 1/3 = ? /6 using paper folding logic.' (2) 'Shade 3/4 of the L-shape drawn on the board.' (3) '12 laddoos shared among 4 children — what fraction does each child get? How many laddoos is that?' (4) 'Is 1/6 greater than 1/8? How do you know?' For each round, students write their answer on a slip and exchange with a partner for a quick peer-check. The relay draws on halves and quarters, non-unit fractions, fractions of collections, and unit-fraction comparison.

Students choose one of three design tasks: (A) Draw a dosa divided into any three toppings and label the fraction of each topping. (B) Draw a garden strip of six equal plots, colour them for two plants, and write the fraction for each. (C) Draw any shape, divide it into six equal parts, shade some of them, and write the fraction shaded and the fraction not shaded — then check: do the two fractions together make a whole? Students work individually and write the fraction names and checks on the same page as the drawing. The choice ensures engagement across different fraction models.

Gallery walk: students leave their drawings on their desks and circulate, reading two neighbours' designs. They place a tick if the fractions are correctly labelled and a question mark if they are unsure. The teacher calls the class back and addresses one or two common question marks on the board, connecting the correction back to the specific idea from the chapter — equal parts, correct denominator, fractions of a collection — that the error touches.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the concrete-to-pictorial journey of the whole chapter: from paper folding that established equal halves and quarters, through the dhokla story that built unit fractions and their inverse ordering, to non-unit fractions in garden strips and dosa circles, fractions of collections, equivalent fractions through folding chains, and the verification of fraction claims in shapes. The relay questions are chosen so that each revisits a different section's core idea; the design task lets students demonstrate understanding through a model they find natural. Watch for persistent confusion between the numerator and denominator roles — a student who writes 4/1 for 'one quarter' is still reading the notation backwards.

Make a flower garden with 7 plots: (a) Marigold in 1/7, Rose and Hibiscus in 3/7 each; (b) Lily in 3/7, Marigold in 2/7, Periwinkle in 2/7; (c) Mogra in 5/7, Hibiscus in 2/7.

tasks.book_ref: Do It Yourself Q1–4 (four dosas), p.73
tasks.description: Write the fractions for each topping in four given dosas (sectors marked with numbers show part size).
Draw flowers in 1/5 of each given group of pots (groups of 5, 10, 15 pots).
Divide the given shapes and shade the appropriate parts: shade 2/3 of rectangle, 4/6 of circle, 1/4 of cross-shape (also show 1/8), 3/4 of L-shape.

tasks.book_ref: Let Us Find Fractions Q1, p.75
tasks.description: 16 barfis divided into 4 equal parts — draw the picture and find how many barfis are in 1/4.

items.section_title: Parts and Wholes — Halves
items.prompt: Draw a square. Draw a line to divide it into two halves. Now draw the same square again and divide it into halves in a different way. Are both your lines correct? How do you know the two parts are equal each time?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A horizontal (or vertical or diagonal) line through the midpoint of the square creates two equal halves; a different line — for example, vertical if the first was horizontal — also creates two equal halves. Both are correct. The student can verify equality by folding the paper so one part sits exactly on top of the other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold or overlap the two parts to check they match exactly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold real paper and trace the fold line; stretch: ask them to find a third way and explain why it works.

exercise.description: Divide the given shapes into halves by drawing a line.

items.section_title: Many Ways to Make Halves and Quarters
items.prompt: Look at the rectangle below. Draw two different lines to show two different ways you could divide it into four equal parts (quarters). Label each part 1/4.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two valid sets of dividing lines that produce four equal parts are correct — for example, three horizontal lines (making four equal horizontal strips) and one horizontal plus one vertical line (making four equal boxes). Each region is labelled 1/4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the rectangle into four equal parts by ensuring each piece has the same area, then label each part 1/4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a printed rectangle to fold physically before drawing; stretch: ask whether they can find a way using diagonal lines.

exercise.description: Draw and show five different ways to fold/cut a rectangle into four equal parts (1/4 or quarter).

items.section_title: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
items.prompt: A round chapati is shared equally among 5 people. What fraction does each person get?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1/5 — the chapati is divided into 5 equal parts and each person receives one part.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide one whole into as many equal parts as there are people; each person's share is 1 divided by that number.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has inverted the fraction, placing the number of people in the numerator rather than the denominator.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused 5 people with 4, possibly recalling the quarters concept from an earlier section.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has written the whole (5/5 = 1) rather than each person's individual share.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a circle divided into 5 slices and shade one; stretch: ask what fraction remains after one person has taken their share.

exercise.description: Shade the dhokla circles to show Sumedha's share for 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, and 9 people; discuss why fractions get smaller as people increase.

items.section_title: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
items.prompt: Ritu cuts a paper strip into equal pieces and gives one piece to her friend. Her friend says the piece is 1/5 of the strip. How many equal pieces did Ritu cut the strip into?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 — if each piece is 1/5, the strip was divided into 5 equal parts.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The denominator of the fraction names the total number of equal parts the whole was divided into.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be thinking of 1 piece given, ignoring the meaning of the denominator.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be confusing 1/5 with 1/4, reading '5' as indicating fourths.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be doubling the denominator, possibly confusing with a halving pattern.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a strip of paper to cut into 5 pieces and hold one up; stretch: ask what fraction the friend would have if Ritu had cut the strip into 8 pieces instead.

exercise.description: Use fraction kit to share observations about pieces and wholes; compare two pieces; verify that 5 pieces of 1/5 make a whole; explain why a given piece is one-third.

items.section_title: Dream Dosa Designer — Fractions of a Whole and Collection
items.prompt: A dosa is divided into 3 equal parts. One part has spicy onion filling and the other two parts have potato filling. Write the fraction of the dosa that has (a) spicy onion filling and (b) potato filling.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 1/3 — one out of three equal parts has spicy onion. (b) 2/3 — two out of three equal parts have potato.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the parts with each filling and write that count over the total number of equal parts.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a circle divided into three sectors and shade them in two colours; stretch: ask the student to check that their two fractions add up to a whole (3/3).

exercise.description: Make a dosa with 2/3 spicy onion and 1/3 classic potato; make another with 3/8 classic potato, 1/8 chilly paneer, 4/8 tangy tomato.

items.section_title: Dream Dosa Designer — Fractions of a Whole and Collection
items.prompt: There are 12 earthen lamps. Priya wants to find 1/4 of them. She divides them into 4 equal groups. How many lamps are in each group?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 — dividing 12 lamps into 4 equal groups gives 3 lamps per group, so 1/4 of 12 is 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total collection into as many equal groups as the denominator; count how many are in one group.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has written the denominator (4) as the answer rather than dividing 12 by 4.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has written the total collection rather than one group's share.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has divided by 2 rather than by 4, finding 1/2 of 12 instead of 1/4.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 12 circles and physically loop groups of 3; stretch: ask the student to find 2/4 of 12 and explain the connection to 1/2.

exercise.description: Meena has 8 diyas — divide into 4 equal groups to find 1/4; colour 2 diyas red.

items.section_title: Equivalent Fractions through Paper Folding
items.prompt: Ananya folded a paper strip into 2 equal parts and coloured one part. She then folded the same strip in half again. Now the strip has 4 parts. How many parts are coloured? Write the new fraction. Is the coloured amount the same as before?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 parts are now coloured. The new fraction is 2/4. Yes, the coloured amount is the same — the strip's coloured region has not changed, only the number of fold lines has increased, so 1/2 = 2/4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: When the strip is folded in half again, both the coloured and total sections double, keeping the coloured fraction the same.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and unfold real paper and count the coloured sections; stretch: ask what the fraction becomes after one more fold (4/8) and whether it is still the same amount.

exercise.description: Fold paper into thirds, colour one third, fold in half repeatedly; observe and write the fraction after each fold: 1/3 = 2/6 = ___ = ___ = ___.

items.section_title: Equivalent Fractions through Paper Folding
items.prompt: A paper strip is folded into 2 equal parts and one part is coloured. The strip is then folded in half, then folded in half once more. Fill in the blanks: 1/2 = 2/4 = ___/8.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4/8. Each time the strip is folded in half, both the coloured sections and the total sections double: 1/2 → 2/4 → 4/8.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: After each fold, both numerator and denominator double, producing an equivalent fraction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student fold real paper and count sections before writing; stretch: continue the chain to the next fold (8/16) and ask what pattern they see.

exercise.description: Fold a new paper starting with two equal parts, halving each time; fill in: 1/2 = 2/4 = ___ = ___ = ___.

items.section_title: Parts and Wholes — Halves
items.prompt: Tara folds a sheet of paper and gets two pieces. She says both pieces are halves. Her friend Mia says they are not halves. The two pieces are not the same size. Who is correct? Explain why in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Mia is correct. For two pieces to be halves, they must be exactly equal in size. If the two pieces are not the same size, neither piece is 1/2 of the whole.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check that both pieces are equal by overlapping or folding one on top of the other.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student two paper pieces of different sizes and ask them to overlap them; stretch: ask the student to fold the paper correctly to get true halves and explain what they did differently.

exercise.description: Discuss which part of the paper you would have chosen (half or two quarters) and why; try with paper; reason about equal division and Samina's choice.

items.section_title: Many Ways to Make Halves and Quarters
items.prompt: A piece of paper is cut into 4 equal parts. One part is shaped like a triangle. What fraction of the whole paper is this triangular piece?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1/4 — the paper is divided into 4 equal parts, so each part, regardless of its shape, is 1/4 of the whole.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The fraction is determined by the number of equal parts the whole is divided into, not by the shape of each part.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing the number of parts (4) with halving, possibly thinking a triangle is half of a square.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be guessing based on the shape (triangle has 3 sides), confusing sides with parts.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has inverted the fraction, placing the total parts in the numerator.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a square cut into 4 triangles and shade one; ask how many total parts there are; stretch: ask whether the fraction would change if the four parts were rectangles instead of triangles.

exercise.description: Match the given part-shapes (hourglass, triangle, semicircle, rectangle) with their corresponding whole shapes using the 1/2 and 1/4 labels.

items.section_title: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
items.prompt: A single gulab jamun is shared equally among 6 children. Later, 2 more children join the group and the gulab jamun is re-shared equally among all 8 children. Does each child get a bigger or smaller share the second time? Write the two fractions and explain.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Smaller share. With 6 children each gets 1/6; with 8 children each gets 1/8. Since 1/8 is less than 1/6 (more people sharing the same whole means each person gets less), the share is smaller the second time.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare unit fractions by remembering that a larger denominator means smaller pieces when the whole is the same.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw two circles each divided into 6 and 8 parts respectively and shade one piece of each; stretch: ask by how many more equal pieces the gulab jamun was split and what pattern they notice.

exercise.description: How much dhokla per person when shared equally among 6 and among 8 people? Who gets bigger pieces? Draw and explain.

items.section_title: Ding Dong Bell — Sharing and Unit Fractions
items.prompt: Which fraction is greater — 1/7 or 1/4?

options.label: A
options.text: 1/4 because when you cut a whole into fewer parts, each part is larger

options.label: C
options.text: 1/7 because 7 pieces fit into the whole more times

options.label: D
options.text: They are equal because the numerators are both 1

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1/4 — dividing a whole into 4 parts gives larger pieces than dividing the same whole into 7 parts.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For unit fractions, the one with the smaller denominator is larger because fewer, bigger pieces make up the whole.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is comparing the digits rather than the size of each part, a classic whole-number reasoning error applied to fractions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly notices equal numerators but wrongly concludes the fractions are therefore equal, ignoring the denominator.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly states that 7 pieces fit into the whole more times but draws the wrong conclusion — more, smaller pieces means each is less.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show two strips side by side, one divided into 4, one into 7, and ask which single piece is bigger; stretch: ask the student to order 1/3, 1/5, and 1/7 from greatest to least and explain.

exercise.description: Fill in blanks to compare unit fractions: which is greater among 1/5 and 1/4; compare 1/9 and 1/6; compare 1/6 and 1/8; choose a pair where one is smaller.

items.section_title: Fractions in Our Surroundings — Collections
items.prompt: Reena's ribbon is 8 cm long. Her ribbon is 1/4 as long as Sunita's ribbon. How long is Sunita's ribbon? Show how you worked it out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sunita's ribbon is 32 cm long. If Reena's 8 cm ribbon is 1/4 of Sunita's, then Sunita's ribbon is 4 times as long: 8 × 4 = 32 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: If the given length is 1/4 of the whole, multiply by 4 to find the whole.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw Reena's ribbon as a short strip and ask the student to draw three more strips of the same length beside it; stretch: ask what fraction of Sunita's ribbon would be 16 cm.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Find Fractions Q2, p.75
exercise.description: Mohan's ribbon is 1/4 as long as Rohan's; given Mohan's ribbon length, draw how long Rohan's ribbon would be.

items.section_title: Equivalent Fractions through Paper Folding
items.prompt: Using a fraction chart that shows strips for halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, and eighths, a student wants to check whether 2 pieces of 1/6 are the same length as 1 piece of 1/3. What does the fraction chart show?

options.label: A
options.text: 2/6 is equal to 1/3 because two 1/6 pieces line up exactly with one 1/3 piece

options.label: B
options.text: 2/6 is greater than 1/3 because 2 is greater than 1

options.label: C
options.text: 2/6 is less than 1/3 because 6 is greater than 3

options.label: D
options.text: The chart cannot be used to compare these fractions

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2/6 is equal to 1/3 — two 1/6 pieces placed side by side span exactly the same length as one 1/3 piece on the chart.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Line up the 1/6 and 1/3 rows of the fraction chart and count how many 1/6 pieces fit into one 1/3 section.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is comparing denominators as whole numbers and concluding larger denominator means larger fraction.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student compares numerators only (2 > 1) and ignores the denominator entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not understand the fraction chart's purpose as a visual comparison tool.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student printed fraction strips to physically place the two 1/6 pieces next to the 1/3 piece; stretch: ask them to find another pair of equivalent fractions on the chart.

exercise.description: Using the fraction chart: how many 1/4 equal 1/2; is 2/3 greater than 1/2; do ten 1/10 make a whole; do three 1/6 equal two 1/8; how many 1/8 make 1/4; find pieces that combine into a bigger piece.

items.section_title: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
items.prompt: Zara shades 3 out of 5 parts of a shape and says the shaded fraction is 3/5. Her friend checks and says the shaded region is NOT 3/5. What is the most likely reason her friend disagrees?

options.label: A
options.text: The 5 parts are not all equal in size, so the fraction 3/5 is not valid

options.label: B
options.text: The fraction should be written as 5/3

options.label: D
options.text: You cannot shade 3 parts of any shape

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The 5 parts are not equal in size, so calling the shaded region 3/5 is not valid — a fraction requires the whole to be divided into equal parts.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A fraction is only valid if the whole is divided into equal parts; unequal parts cannot be named as equal fractions.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses the role of numerator and denominator, thinking the numerator should equal the total.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has a misconception that shading three parts is somehow not allowed, showing a lack of understanding of fraction notation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student inverts the fraction without understanding why.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw two squares — one cut into 5 equal parts, one into 5 unequal parts — and ask which one can use fractions; stretch: ask the student to redraw the unequal shape with equal parts and re-verify the fraction.

exercise.description: Check whether Ameena, Kishore, Perry, Kunj, Balu, and Gita's fraction claims for shaded regions are correct; circle correct ones, cross out incorrect; draw lines to make parts equal if needed.

items.section_title: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
items.prompt: A set of 8 tiles is arranged in a row. Three tiles are blue, the rest are yellow. What fraction of the tiles is blue? What fraction is yellow? Do the two fractions together make a whole? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3/8 of the tiles are blue; 5/8 are yellow. Together: 3/8 + 5/8 = 8/8 = 1 whole. Yes, the two fractions make a whole.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the blue tiles for the numerator and the total tiles for the denominator; repeat for yellow; check that the two fractions sum to 8/8.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 8 squares and colour 3 blue, then count the yellow ones; stretch: ask the student to write a different pair of fractions that together make a whole using 10 tiles.

exercise.description: Identify the fraction of the whole that the blue parts make in each of three pattern-block pictures (hexagons, diamonds, arrow shapes).

items.section_title: Many Ways to Make Halves and Quarters
items.prompt: A square is divided into 4 parts. Which of the following is true for it to show quarters correctly?

options.label: A
options.text: The 4 parts must all be equal in size

options.label: B
options.text: The 4 parts must all be triangles

options.label: C
options.text: The 4 parts must be arranged in a row

options.label: D
options.text: The 4 parts must be the same shape as the whole

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The 4 parts must all be equal in size. Quarters require equal parts regardless of shape or arrangement.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A quarter (1/4) means one of four equal parts; equality of size, not shape, is the requirement.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses shape with fraction — parts can be any shape as long as they are equal.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student incorrectly believes parts must replicate the shape of the whole.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student introduces a non-requirement about arrangement.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show two squares, one divided into 4 equal rectangles and one into 4 unequal triangles, and ask which shows quarters; stretch: ask the student to find two different shapes that each part can be while still showing correct quarters.

exercise.description: Divide the given shapes (diamond, rectangle, oval, L-shape, cross-shape) into 4 equal parts/quarters.

items.section_title: My Flower Garden — Non-unit Fractions
items.prompt: A garden strip has 6 equal plots. Sunflower plants are in 4 of the plots and marigold plants are in the rest. Write the fraction for sunflower plots and the fraction for marigold plots.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sunflower: 4/6. Marigold: 2/6. (The remaining 2 plots out of 6 have marigold.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the plots for each plant and write that count over the total number of plots.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 6 boxes, shade 4 for sunflowers, count the rest for marigolds; stretch: ask the student whether any two fractions in this problem are equivalent to simpler fractions they know.

exercise.description: Make a flower garden with 7 plots: (a) Marigold in 1/7, Rose and Hibiscus in 3/7 each; (b) Lily in 3/7, Marigold in 2/7, Periwinkle in 2/7; (c) Mogra in 5/7, Hibiscus in 2/7.

items.section_title: Dream Dosa Designer — Fractions of a Whole and Collection
items.prompt: A dosa is divided into 8 equal sectors. The fraction for chutney topping is 3/8. How many sectors have chutney?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 sectors have chutney — the numerator 3 counts the number of sectors with that topping.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The numerator of the fraction tells how many equal parts are named.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student reads the denominator as the answer, confusing the total parts with the counted parts.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student subtracts: 8 − 3 = 5, finding the sectors without chutney instead of those with it.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing unit fraction thinking and writing 1 as the numerator for any fraction.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a circle with 8 sectors and shade 3; count the shaded ones; stretch: ask the student to write the fraction for the sectors that do NOT have chutney.

exercise.book_ref: Do It Yourself Q1–4 (four dosas), p.73
exercise.description: Write the fractions for each topping in four given dosas (sectors marked with numbers show part size).

items.section_title: Fractions in Our Surroundings — Collections
items.prompt: There are 15 pots in a row. Flowers are planted in 1/5 of the pots. How many pots have flowers?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 pots. Dividing 15 pots into 5 equal groups gives 3 pots per group; 1/5 of 15 = 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total count by the denominator to find one group; that is 1/5.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 15 circles and loop groups of 3; count one group; stretch: ask how many pots have flowers if 2/5 of the pots are planted.

exercise.description: Draw flowers in 1/5 of each given group of pots (groups of 5, 10, 15 pots).

items.section_title: Identifying and Shading Fractions in Figures
items.prompt: Draw a rectangle and divide it into 3 equal parts. Shade 2 parts. Write the fraction you have shaded.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2/3. The rectangle is divided into 3 equal parts and 2 are shaded, so the shaded fraction is 2/3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count shaded parts for the numerator and total equal parts for the denominator.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a printed rectangle with three faint guide lines already drawn; stretch: ask the student to also write the fraction that is not shaded and check that the two fractions total 3/3.

exercise.description: Divide the given shapes and shade the appropriate parts: shade 2/3 of rectangle, 4/6 of circle, 1/4 of cross-shape (also show 1/8), 3/4 of L-shape.

items.section_title: Fractions in Our Surroundings — Collections
items.prompt: 18 laddoos are shared equally among 6 children. What fraction of the laddoos does each child get? How many laddoos does each child receive?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each child gets 1/6 of the laddoos, which is 3 laddoos (18 ÷ 6 = 3).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 18 by 6 to find each child's share; write the fraction as 1/6 and the count as 3.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 18 circles and loop them into 6 groups of 3; stretch: ask what fraction each child would get if only 4 children shared the same 18 laddoos, and whether each child gets more or fewer laddoos.

exercise.description: 12 cookies shared equally; find the fraction each child gets for 3, 6, 2, and 4 children.

items.section_title: Fractions in Our Surroundings — Collections
items.prompt: 20 mithai pieces are divided into 4 equal groups. How many mithai pieces are in 1/4 of the collection?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 mithai pieces. 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so 1/4 of 20 is 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total by the denominator to find the number of pieces in one equal group.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 20 small squares and physically circle groups of 5; stretch: ask how many pieces are in 3/4 of the collection and explain the reasoning.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Find Fractions Q1, p.75
exercise.description: 16 barfis divided into 4 equal parts — draw the picture and find how many barfis are in 1/4.
